extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for running effective office hours and training instructors to provide meaningful one-on-one mathematics teaching; includes meeting plans, goals, practice activities, and strategies to encourage student attendance and assess understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposes of office hours
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary functions of one-on-one teaching during office hours (beyond individualized instruction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office hours can: alleviate mathematics anxiety; motivate and nurture students; aid retention; provide feedback for both student and instructor; model expert problem solving; detect and fill gaps in prior knowledge; teach study skills (e.g., assessing an answer for correctness); motivate struggling students; encourage broader interest in mathematics; give make-up quizzes or proﬁciency exams; help instructors get to know students personally; provide focused assessment opportunities and immediate feedback; prompt the instructor to find alternative explanations; and shift students' perception of mathematics toward a way of thinking rather than a set of rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals for an instructor-training meeting on office hours
rubrics_metrics.description: What an instructor-training session about office hours should accomplish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide institutional/departmental guidelines on office hours; encourage instructors to think about reasons for holding office hours and ways to encourage student attendance; give instructors opportunity to practice one-on-one teaching; create a forum to discuss what makes a successful office-hour encounter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation for an office-hours training meeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Materials and preparatory steps leaders should take before running a training meeting about office hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather institutional/departmental office-hour guidelines; choose a representative textbook problem a student might bring; make copies of readings on one-on-one teaching; circulate the agenda in advance; prepare meeting materials and questionnaires; confirm attendance with participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda for an office-hours training meeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested major agenda items to distribute to participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss the importance of quality one-on-one teaching; discuss opinions/experiences of office hours; brainstorm ideas to get students to attend; discuss effective one-on-one teaching and run a practice office-hour encounter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-structured outline for running the meeting
rubrics_metrics.description: A fifty-minute, time-segmented outline for the training meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce and review agenda (:01–:05); discuss roles and reasons for office hours (:05–:15) including list of functions; have participants complete 'Opinions of Office Hours' and discuss motivations and barriers (:15–:25); review 'Ideas for Getting Students to Come to Office Hours' or brainstorm alternatives; practice one-on-one teaching with role-plays and observer feedback (:25–:45); wrap up with summary, questions, readings, or a questionnaire (:45–:50).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing and enhancing student understanding in office hours
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles for what to do (and not do) when helping a student during office hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Get the student to think rather than doing the thinking for them; concentrate on the problem-solving process more than just the correct answer; encourage student reflection on what is being learned and how it connects to other course material; make the student do the writing (do not pick up the pencil); ask probing questions that assess understanding; have the student work on a related but slightly different problem; give problem-solving strategy advice while refraining from solving the problem yourself; encourage and reassure the student.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategies to encourage students to attend office hours
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical tactics instructors can use to increase student attendance at office hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hold some office hours in attractive or informal environments (coffee bar, lounge); announce targeted office hours focused on a known difficult portion of an assignment; hold hours in public computer sites when relevant; when grading, invite students to attend with a correction and note about future importance; remind students at end of class about office hours; offer special sessions to build a habit of coming (e.g., how to use tools); give each visiting student at least one affirmative comment; when not busy, ask visiting students how the course is going to build connection; schedule hours at varied times and be willing to meet by appointment if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role-play structure for office-hour practice
rubrics_metrics.description: How to organize and run role-play practice during the training meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count instructors into groups of three; assign roles of student, instructor (listener), and observer; give instructors and students a copy of the exercise and observers an 'Office Hour Workshop Observer Checklist'; have students approximate realistic stuck behavior; allow about ten minutes for role-play including set-up; follow with a five-minute group discussion based on observer notes; discuss particularly effective instructor behaviors and reflections on problem-solving teaching strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling reluctance to role-play
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategies to get reluctant instructors to participate in role-plays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge the artificiality but emphasize the practice opportunity; stress that role-playing is voluntary but only works if everyone participates; allow switching assignments if someone cannot play student or instructor; as an alternative, use a vignette and the checklist for discussion, recognizing that vignettes miss nonverbal cues and practice opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observer checklist item: prompt student to read/state the problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Observer should note whether the instructor prompts the student to read or state the problem aloud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tally occurrences. This encourages clarity, helps the student focus and reveals their understanding of the problem statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observer checklist item: encourage the student to think aloud
rubrics_metrics.description: Observer should note whether the instructor encourages the student to verbalize their thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tally occurrences. Thinking aloud helps the instructor assess reasoning, identify misconceptions, and guide without doing the work for the student.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observer checklist item: ask for examples/explanations/clarification
rubrics_metrics.description: Observer should note whether the instructor elicits information, examples, or clarification from the student.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tally occurrences. Asking for clarification probes the student's conceptual understanding and helps tailor assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observer checklist item: offer information/examples/explanations/clarification
rubrics_metrics.description: Observer should note whether the instructor offers needed information or explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tally occurrences. Providing targeted explanations can unblock students, but should be balanced to avoid doing the problem for them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observer checklist item: offer problem-solving advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Observer should note whether the instructor offers strategy-level advice (heuristics, approaches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tally occurrences. Advice should aim at improving problem-solving skill rather than giving a direct solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observer checklist item: paraphrase or summarize student reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Observer should note whether the instructor paraphrases or summarizes what the student said.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tally occurrences. Paraphrasing helps check and clarify understanding and models reflective practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observer checklist item: give reassurance or praise
rubrics_metrics.description: Observer should note whether the instructor provides reassurance or positive feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tally occurrences. Reassurance and praise build students' confidence and encourage future attendance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observer checklist item: record who actually solved the problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Observer should note whether the problem was solved by the student or the instructor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a key evaluative metric: if the instructor solved it, the encounter may have been less effective at building student problem-solving skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office-hour vignette interaction practices (illustrated by transcript)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete conversational techniques demonstrated in the vignette transcript of an instructor-student interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask the student to read the problem; identify units to infer variable types (e.g., volume vs. height); ask what the student has done so far and have them write key formulas; identify related variables and relationships before differentiating (e.g., relate r and h); simplify algebra before differentiating; remind to include units when reporting rates. Use questioning to lead student to relate variables and complete the problem themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meeting materials for office-hours training
rubrics_metrics.description: Materials to prepare and bring to the training meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copies of 'Opinions of Office Hours' handout; 'Ideas for Getting Students to Come to Office Hours' handout; 'Office Hour Workshop Observer Checklist'; copies of a representative textbook problem for role-play; 'Office Hours Vignette' if using vignette alternative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of classroom-control difficulties
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytical framework to categorize classroom control issues in interactive mathematics classrooms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Four categories: (1) Implicit, mismatched ideas of course expectations between instructor and students (attendance, grading expectations); (2) Difficulties arising from the nature of an interactive classroom (opportunities for students to affect pace/direction leading to off-task behavior); (3) Difficulties between individual students and the administrative structure of the course (e.g., requests about exam scheduling that conflict with policy); (4) Highly interpersonal situations between students and instructor (belligerence, grade disputes) — often requiring different handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and goals for a meeting on classroom control
rubrics_metrics.description: What an instructor-training meeting on classroom control should aim to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an analytical framework for categorizing control difficulties; have participants share uncomfortable experiences; help participants realize they are not alone; generate workable solutions; alert those without experience that such problems can occur; provide opportunities for reflection and planning alternative actions for future classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation for a classroom-control training meeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Steps leaders should take to prepare a meeting on classroom control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find out what control issues participants face via interviews or surveys (or classroom visits); set tone to allow candid sharing (use prewritten scenarios that are recognizable but not exposing); consider inviting experienced instructors who have faced and recovered from control issues; research literature on assertiveness and classroom behavior to synthesize relevant strategies; plan to end the meeting on a positive note (e.g., summarize successes or constructive next steps).
